newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia unveils steady mid-term budget.
newsitem.headline: Australia unveils steady mid-term budget.

text.p: Australia's conservative government unveiled a cautious mid-term budget on Tuesday, making modest spending cuts but offering a tax break to voters to kick in just before the next election.

Treasurer Peter Costello projected a higher-than-expected underlying deficit -- excluding windfalls such as asset sales -- of A$3.85 billion (US$3 billion) for the fiscal year from July, down from A$6.86 billion in 1996/97.
Costello told parliament the budget would improve the climate for business, boost economic growth and help combat stubborn joblessness.
Budget cuts amount to just A$352 million, well down on market forecasts of up to A$1.5 billion, and economists had expected the deficit to be pared back to about A$2 billion.
But Costello said the cuts would be enough to achieve an underlying surplus of A$1.597 billion in 1998/99, the first since 1990/91, and well ahead of the targetted budget balance.

The biggest carrot in the budget statement was a 15-percent tax rebate on savings interest targetted at middle Australia. But that scheme, to cost A$350 million in the first year, won't begin to kick in until 1998/99, just ahead of the next election due in early 1999.
It was also less than previously promised.
Costello said the government had met its promise of turning Australia's finances around from deficit to surplus in its first term and set the country on the path to prosperity.

"The story on the economy is a good one -- we're forecasting a pick-up in growth, a pick up in employment ... and very favourable prospects not just I think for this year, but for the years ahead," he told reporters.
"Australia is now paying its way again. This is a very good effort by world standards."
Costello said the budget was responsible and would be welcomed by financial markets.
"This a government which is going to set goals and deliver," he said. "The days of the rabbit out of the hat are over."
With asset sales and other one-off items, the budget's bottom line for 1997/98 will be a surplus of A$6.423 billion, or 1.2 percent of gross domestic product.
The budget carried some pain -- notably higher medicine costs and a little-improved outlook for unemployment -- but was unlikely to spook voters.

Prime Minister John Howard, whose popularity has fallen sharply in recent weeks, had looked to the budget to help break a slide in opinion polls, distract voters from a divisive land rights row and check the surging popularity of right-wing politician Pauline Hason.

A newspaper poll published earlier on Tuesday showed the government's support at 40 percent, just one point ahead of the Labor opposition and compared with a steady 12-point lead for most of the past 14 months since the last election.
Hanson's newly-formed One Nation Party increased two points over the past week to nine percent -- five points ahead of the traditional third political force, the Australian Democrats.
The budget forecast accelerating but modest economic growth of 3.75 percent and continuing low inflation of one percent.

But there was little joy for the unemployed. Although a work for welfare scheme will be implemented to help the jobless gain work skills, the unemployment rate is tipped to fall only marginally to 8.25 percent, year-average, from 8.75 percent.

There were two big ticket items -- a special A$1.25 billion environmental fund, to be funded by the proceeds of the one-third privatisation of telecomms carrier Telstra, and a A$1 billion fund to pay for celebrations to mark the 2001 centenary of Australian statehood.
